claim: A quantitative analysis of starvation-induced proteome remodeling in yeast reveals comprehensive changes already in the first three hours.
source: A quantitative analysis of starvation-induced proteome remodeling in yeast reveals comprehensive changes already in the first three hours.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, which is supported by the SILAC-based proteomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many different integral plasma membrane proteins undergo endocytosis and degradation in vacuoles via the multivesicular body (MVB) pathway during the first three hours of starvation.
source: In this period, many different integral plasma membrane proteins undergo endocytosis and degradation in vacuoles via the multivesicular body (MVB) pathway.
evidence: The manuscript presents proteomic data showing down-regulation of multiple plasma membrane proteins and microscopy data showing their delivery to vacuoles.

claim: The degradation of plasma membrane proteins via the MVB pathway becomes essential to maintain critical amino acid levels that uphold protein synthesis early during starvation.
source: Their degradation becomes essential to maintain critical amino acids levels that uphold protein synthesis early during starvation.
evidence: The manuscript presents amino acid measurements and protein synthesis assays showing that vps4∆ mutants have lower amino acid levels and reduced protein synthesis.

claim: The MVB pathway promotes cellular adaptation, including the de novo synthesis of vacuolar hydrolases to boost the vacuolar catabolic activity.
source: This promotes cellular adaptation, including the de novo synthesis of vacuolar hydrolases to boost the vacuolar catabolic activity.
evidence: The manuscript shows proteomic data of increased vacuolar hydrolase levels and Pho8 activity assays demonstrating increased catabolic activity.

claim: The order of events involving the MVB pathway primes vacuoles for the efficient degradation of bulk cytoplasm via autophagy.
source: This order of events primes vacuoles for the efficient degradation of bulk cytoplasm via autophagy.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing delayed degradation of autophagic cargo in vps4∆ mutants and demonstrates the temporal sequence of MVB pathway and autophagy activation.

claim: A catabolic cascade including the coordinated action of the MVB pathway and autophagy is essential to enter quiescence to survive extended periods of nutrient limitation.
source: Hence, a catabolic cascade including the coordinated action of the MVB pathway and autophagy is essential to enter quiescence to survive extended periods of nutrient limitation.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on cell cycle arrest (bud index) and survival assays showing that both pathways are required for quiescence and survival.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) mediates selective poly-ubiquitination of cytoplasmic proteins and their degradation at 26S proteasomes for regulatory and quality control functions.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) mediates selective poly-ubiquitination of cytoplasmic proteins and their degradation at 26S proteasomes for regulatory and quality control functions.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the UPS system.

claim: Mis-folded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are ubiquitinated, extracted by the ER-associated protein degradation system (ERAD) and degraded at 26S proteasomes in the cytoplasm.
source: Mis-folded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are also ubiquitinated, extracted by the ER-associated protein degradation system (ERAD) and degraded at 26S proteasomes in the cytoplasm (Vembar and Brodsky, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Under normal growth conditions autophagy operates on a basal level because it is suppressed by signaling from the target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1).
source: Therefore the induction of autophagy is tightly controlled: under normal growth conditions autophagy operates on a basal level because it is suppressed by signaling from the target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1) (Kamada et al., 2000; Loewith and Hall, 2011; Zoncu et al., 2011b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In response to cellular stress, such as nutrient depletion, TORC1 is inactivated and autophagy is strongly induced.
source: In response to cellular stress, such as nutrient depletion (e.g., of amino acids), TORC1 is inactivated (Loewith and Hall, 2011) and autophagy is strongly induced.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Deregulation of autophagic processes is implicated in metabolic and infectious diseases as well as in cancer or neurodegeneration.
source: Deregulation of autophagic processes is implicated in metabolic and infectious diseases as well as in cancer or neurodegeneration (Rubinsztein et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Once induced, the autophagic machinery begins to sequester cytoplasmic components, ribosomes and organelles within a large double-membrane compartment termed the autophagosome.
source: Once induced, the autophagic machinery begins to sequester cytoplasmic components, ribosomes and organelles within a large double-membrane compartment termed the autophagosome (Yang and Klionsky, 2010; Kraft and Martens, 2012; Mizushima et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some core components of the autophagic machinery such as LC3/Atg8 are transcriptionally induced.
source: In addition, some core components of the autophagic machinery such as LC3/Atg8 are transcriptionally induced (Kirisako et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Direct fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes delivers autophagic bodies and the sequestered cargo into the lysosomal lumen.
source: Direct fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes delivers autophagic bodies and the sequestered cargo into the lysosomal lumen.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about autophagy.

claim: Autophagosomes can first fuse with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) to form so-called amphisomes, before they fuse with lysosomes.
source: Alternatively, autophagosomes can first fuse with multivesicular bodies (MVBs) to form so-called amphisomes, before they fuse with lysosomes (Seglen et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The breakdown of autophagic bodies and the efficient degradation of autophagic cargo inside lysosomes is required to recycle amino acids, nucleotides, carbohydrates and lipids back to the cytoplasm.
source: Finally, the breakdown of autophagic bodies and the efficient degradation of autophagic cargo inside lysosomes is required to recycle amino acids, nucleotides, carbohydrates and lipids back to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about lysosomal degradation.

claim: The recycling of key metabolic building blocks protects cells from their fatal depletion and thus maintains cellular homeostasis to survive nutrient limitation.
source: The recycling of these key metabolic building blocks protects cells from their fatal depletion and thus maintains cellular homeostasis to survive nutrient limitation (Onodera and Ohsumi, 2005; Vabulas and Hartl, 2005; Jones et al., 2012; Suraweera et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Evolutionary conserved starvation programs in mammalian cells and yeast expand and strengthen the intracellular recycling system by enhancing the de novo synthesis of vacuolar/lysosomal hydrolases.
source: Therefore evolutionary conserved starvation programs in mammalian cells and yeast expand and strengthen this intracellular recycling system by enhancing the de novo synthesis of vacuolar/lysosomal hydrolases (Gasch et al., 2000; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011; Shen and Mizushima, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TORC1 signaling was required to promote the endocytosis of certain plasma membrane proteins.
source: On the one hand, TORC1 signaling was required to promote the endocytosis of certain plasma membrane proteins (MacGurn et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of TORC1 either by rapamycin or starvation triggered the endocytosis of other plasma membrane proteins that were subsequently degraded in an ESCRT-dependent manner via the MVB pathway.
source: On the other hand, inactivation of TORC1 either by rapamycin or starvation, triggered the endocytosis of other plasma membrane proteins that were subsequently degraded in an ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport)-dependent manner via the MVB pathway (Schmidt et al., 1998; Jones et al., 2012; Lang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Within 3 hr after the onset of starvation the majority of Mup1-GFP was removed from the cell surface, delivered into vacuoles and degraded.
source: Yet, within 3 hr after the onset of starvation the majority of Mup1-GFP was removed from the cell surface, delivered into vacuoles and degraded (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and microscopy data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The proteolytic degradation of Mup1-GFP inside vacuoles released free GFP, which remained stable and was monitored by western blotting.
source: The proteolytic degradation of Mup1-GFP inside vacuoles released free GFP, which remained stable and was monitored by western blotting (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The starvation-induced delivery of Mup1-GFP into the vacuole was dependent on the ESCRT machinery but was not affected in an autophagy (atg8∆) mutant.
source: The starvation-induced delivery of Mup1-GFP into the vacuole was dependent on the ESCRT machinery but was not affected in an autophagy (atg8∆) mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In an ESCRT (vps4∆) mutant, the MVB pathway was blocked and Mup1-GFP was not delivered into the vacuole but instead accumulated on the class E compartment and at the plasma membrane.
source: In an ESCRT (vps4∆) mutant, the MVB pathway was blocked and Mup1-GFP was not delivered into the vacuole but instead accumulated on the class E compartment and at the plasma membrane (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Growing yeast cells contain about 200,000 ribosomes that occupy up to 30–40% of the cytoplasmic volume.
source: Growing yeast cells contain about 200,000 ribosomes that occupy up to 30–40% of the cytoplasmic volume (Warner, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Upon starvation, otherwise stable ribosomes are among the first autophagic cargoes and rapidly degraded by selective (ribophagy) and non-selective autophagy.
source: Upon starvation, otherwise stable ribosomes are among the first autophagic cargoes and rapidly degraded by selective (ribophagy) and non-selective autophagy (Kraft et al., 2008; Ossareh-Nazari et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After 3 hr of starvation, at a time when the majority of full length Mup1-GFP was already degraded, free GFP from Rpl25 was first detected, showing that autophagy was also delivering cytoplasmic contents into the vacuole.
source: After 3 hr, at a time when the majority of full length Mup1-GFP was already degraded, free GFP from Rpl25 was first detected, showing that autophagy was also delivering cytoplasmic contents into the vacuole (Figure 1A, lane 8).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Small amounts of free GFP released from GFP-Atg8 inside vacuoles could be readily detected by western blot analysis 1 hr after the onset of starvation and the levels of free GFP strongly increased at 3 hr of starvation.
source: Small amounts of free GFP released from GFP-Atg8 inside vacuoles could be readily detected by western blot analysis 1 hr after the onset of starvation and the levels of free GFP strongly increased at 3 hr of starvation (Figure 1A, lane 27–30).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Atg8 protein levels control the size of autophagosomes but not the frequency (about 9 autophagosomes/hour) by which they are formed.
source: Previous work also demonstrated that Atg8 protein levels control the size of autophagosomes but not the frequency (about 9 autophagosomes/hour) by which they are formed (Abeliovich et al., 2000; Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pho8∆60 activity was low under rich conditions, began to increase during the first 3 hr of starvation and continuously increased during extended periods of starvation.
source: Pho8∆60 activity was low under rich conditions, began to increase during the first 3 hr of starvation and continuously increased during extended periods of starvation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Pho8∆60 activity assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Autophagy is immediately activated upon starvation and delivers increasing volumes of cytoplasmic material into the vacuole with ongoing starvation.
source: These results show that autophagy is immediately activated upon starvation and delivers increasing volumes of cytoplasmic material into the vacuole with ongoing starvation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by multiple assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ub-GFP is an established reporter for proteasomal activity.
source: Therefore, we employed a ubiquitin-GFP (Ub-GFP) fusion protein, which is an established reporter for proteasomal activity (Johnson et al., 1992; Vabulas and Hartl, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon starvation, Ub-GFP was rapidly degraded at 26S proteasomes.
source: Upon starvation, Ub-GFP was rapidly degraded at 26S proteasomes.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The degradation of the Ub-GFP reporter was exclusively dependent on proteasomal degradation but did not require autophagy or the MVB pathway.
source: The degradation of the reporter was exclusively dependent on proteasomal degradation but did not require autophagy or the MVB pathway (Figure 1C, lanes 5–7; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Starvation triggered protein degradation by different selective and non-selective degradation pathways: the constitutive protein degradation via the proteasome was active from the onset of starvation.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that starvation triggered protein degradation by different selective and non-selective degradation pathways: the constitutive protein degradation via the proteasome was active from the onset of starvation and was previously suggested to play a key role upon acute nutrient restriction (Vabulas and Hartl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the Ub-GFP degradation data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Both autophagy and starvation induced-endocytosis were simultaneously activated early during starvation.
source: Our results further suggest that both autophagy and starvation induced-endocytosis were simultaneously activated early during starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing data presented for Mup1-GFP degradation and GFP-Atg8 degradation.

claim: Autophagy continuously delivered ever-increasing volumes of cytoplasm into vacuoles, whereas the starvation-induced degradation of membrane proteins was completed within 3 hr.
source: Autophagy continuously delivered ever-increasing volumes of cytoplasm into vacuoles, whereas the starvation-induced degradation of membrane proteins was completed within 3 hr.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing data presented for various degradation reporters.

claim: When grown in synthetic medium supplemented with amino acids (rich), the intracellular free amino acid levels were comparable in WT cells and autophagy mutants (atg8∆).
source: When grown in synthetic medium supplemented with amino acids (rich), the intracellular free amino acid levels were comparable in WT cells and autophagy mutants (atg8∆) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Intracellular free amino acid levels were slightly lower in vps4∆ mutants under rich conditions, which was mainly due to reduced lysine and arginine levels.
source: but slightly lower in vps4∆ mutants, which was mainly due to reduced lysine and arginine levels (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: 1 hr after starvation, the total free amino acid pool decreased to similar levels in WT cells and all mutant strains.
source: 1 hr after starvation in synthetic medium without amino acids and ammonium salts, the total free amino acid pool decreased to similar levels in WT cells and all mutant strains (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: In WT cells the levels of most amino acids continued to decrease for another hour after starvation.
source: In WT cells the levels of most amino acids continued to decrease for another hour.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: At around 4 hr of starvation the overall levels of amino acids almost fully recovered in WT cells, suggesting strong amino acid recycling.
source: Interestingly, at around 4 hr of starvation the overall levels of amino acids almost fully recovered, suggesting strong amino acid recycling.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The recovery of amino acid levels after 4 hr of starvation was strongly dependent on autophagy.
source: The recovery of amino acid levels after 4 hr of starvation was strongly dependent on autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data in atg8∆ mutants shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: After 2 hr of starvation the overall amino acid levels were lower in vps4∆ mutants compared to WT cells and autophagy mutants.
source: However, after 2 hr the overall amino acid levels were lower in vps4∆ mutants compared to WT cells and autophagy mutants.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The levels of 14 individual amino acids were lower in vps4∆ mutants when compared to WT cells or autophagy mutants after 2 hr of starvation.
source: The levels of 14 individual amino acids were lower in vps4∆ mutants when compared to WT cells or autophagy mutants.
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The amino acid levels failed to recover during extended starvation in vps4∆ mutants.
source: Moreover the amino acid levels failed to recover during extended starvation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: From 2 hr onwards, the amino acid levels were always lowest in the double mutants (vps4∆, atg8∆).
source: From 2 hr onwards, the amino acid levels were always lowest in the double mutants (vps4∆, atg8∆) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The MVB pathway is essential to maintain the levels of most free intracellular amino acids within the first 2 hr of starvation, while autophagy is essential to restore intracellular amino acids later during starvation.
source: These results showed that the MVB pathway was essential to maintain the levels of most free intracellular amino acids within the first 2 hr of starvation, while autophagy was essential to restore intracellular amino acids later during starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid measurement data in different mutants.

claim: Under rich conditions, 35S-label incorporation was comparable in WT cells, atg8∆ and vps4∆ single or double mutants.
source: Under rich conditions, 35S-label incorporation was comparable in WT cells, atg8∆ and vps4∆ single or double mutants (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Already 1 hr after starvation, 35S-label incorporation was reduced to 40% in WT cells.
source: Already 1 hr after starvation, 35S-label incorporation was reduced to 40% in WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: During the next 3 hr of starvation, WT cells managed to maintain protein synthesis at 40% of rich conditions.
source: During the next 3 hr of starvation, WT cells managed to maintain protein synthesis at this level (Figure 2C, lanes 1, 5, 9,13, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In the autophagy-deficient atg8∆ mutant, 35S-label incorporation was initially similar to WT cells for up to 2 hr, but began to decline after 4 hr of starvation.
source: In the autophagy-deficient atg8∆ mutant, 35S-label incorporation was initially similar to WT cells for up to 2 hr, but began to decline after 4 hr of starvation (Figure 2C, lanes 3, 7, 11, 15, Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In ESCRT mutants (vps4∆), protein synthesis declined faster when compared to WT cells or autophagy mutants.
source: In ESCRT mutants (vps4∆), protein synthesis declined faster when compared to WT cells or autophagy mutants, which seems consistent with the more rapid decline of intracellular amino acids (Figure 2C, lanes 2, 6, 10, 14, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: vps4∆, atg8∆ double mutants showed an additive effect, since even less 35S-label was incorporated upon starvation compared to the single deletion mutants.
source: vps4∆, atg8∆ double mutants showed an additive effect, since even less 35S-label was incorporated upon starvation compared to the single deletion mutants (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by 35S-incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The MVB pathway is essential to maintain a critical pool of free amino acids for protein synthesis early during starvation.
source: Taken together these findings suggest that (i) the MVB pathway is essential to maintain a critical pool of free amino acids for protein synthesis early during starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid and protein synthesis data in vps4∆ mutants.

claim: In the absence of the MVB pathway autophagy can only partially uphold amino acids levels and protein synthesis.
source: (ii) In the absence of the MVB pathway autophagy can only partially uphold amino acids levels and protein synthesis
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid and protein synthesis data in vps4∆ mutants.

claim: The MVB pathway and autophagy cooperate to maintain intracellular amino acids during starvation, potentially in a consecutive manner.
source: (iii) The MVB pathway and autophagy cooperate to maintain intracellular amino acids during starvation, potentially in a consecutive manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid and protein synthesis data in different mutants.

claim: Under nutrient rich growth conditions, TORC1 was active and its direct targets Sch9 and Atg13 were phosphorylated in WT cells, vps4∆ and atg8∆ mutants.
source: Under nutrient rich growth conditions, TORC1 was active and its direct targets Sch9 and Atg13 were phosphorylated in WT cells, vps4∆ and atg8∆ mutants (Figure 3A,B, lane 1, 3, 5) (Kamada et al., 2000; Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A,B and citations to prior work.

claim: When autophagy and the MVB pathway were simultaneously disrupted (vps4∆, atg8∆), TORC1 signaling appeared to be reduced under rich growth conditions, but not completely switched off.
source: When autophagy and the MVB pathway were simultaneously disrupted (vps4∆, atg8∆), TORC1 signaling appeared to be reduced under rich growth conditions, but not completely switched off (Figure 3A, lane 7).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Upon starvation TORC1 signaling was efficiently turned off and the autophagy core component Atg13 was dephosphorylated in all strains, which is a prerequisite for the induction of autophagy.
source: Upon starvation TORC1 signaling was efficiently turned off and the autophagy core component Atg13 was dephosphorylated in all strains, which is a prerequisite for the induction of autophagy (Figure 3B) (Kamada et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to prior work.

claim: Upon starvation, GFP-Atg8 was efficiently transported into the lumen of vacuoles in WT cells and vps4∆ mutants.
source: Upon starvation, GFP-Atg8 was efficiently transported into the lumen of vacuoles in WT cells and vps4∆ mutants (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The autophagic machinery was fully operational and independent of the ESCRT machinery.
source: indicating that the autophagic machinery was fully operational and independent of the ESCRT machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the GFP-Atg8 transport data in vps4∆ mutants.

claim: Pho8∆60 activity increased after 4 hr of starvation in WT and vps4∆ mutants, but not in atg8∆ cells.
source: Pho8∆60 activity increased after 4 hr of starvation in WT and vps4∆ mutants, but not in atg8∆ cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Pho8∆60 activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In yeast autophagosomes together with their cargo were delivered into the vacuoles of vps4∆ mutants in response to starvation.
source: Collectively, these results show that in yeast autophagosomes together with their cargo were delivered into the vacuoles of vps4∆ mutants in response to starvation, which is consistent with earlier reports (Reggiori et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the GFP-Atg8 and Pho8∆60 data and a citation to prior work.

claim: The lysis of autophagic bodies depends on vacuolar acidification, the catabolic activity of Pep4 and Prb1 and the lipase Atg15.
source: This is a prerequisite for the subsequent proteolytic breakdown of autophagic cargo (Takeshige et al., 1992; Yang et al., 2006) and depends on vacuolar acidification, the catabolic activity of Pep4 and Prb1 and the lipase Atg15 (Teter et al., 2000; Epple et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In WT cells the fluorescence of pHluorin-Atg8 was efficiently quenched in the lumen of vacuoles upon starvation (>90% of cells, n = 157).
source: In WT cells the fluorescence of pHluorin-Atg8 was efficiently quenched in the lumen of vacuoles upon starvation (>90% of cells, n = 157).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In mutants that are either deficient in vacuolar peptidases (prb1∆, prc1∆, pep4∆) or vacuolar acidification (vma4∆) pHluorin-Atg8 was not quenched (<10% of cells, n = 198 and n = 40, respectively) and pHluorin-Atg8 positive vesicular structures were detected inside their vacuoles, suggesting that autophagic bodies were not efficiently lysed.
source: In contrast, in mutants that are either deficient in vacuolar peptidases (prb1∆, prc1∆, pep4∆) or vacuolar acidification (vma4∆) pHluorin-Atg8 was not quenched (<10% of cells, n = 198 and n = 40, respectively) and pHluorin-Atg8 positive vesicular structures were detected inside their vacuoles, suggesting that autophagic bodies were not efficiently lysed (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In the vast majority of vps4∆ mutants (>90% of cells, n = 121), the fluorescence of pHluorin-Atg8 was quenched in the vacuoles similar to WT cells.
source: In the vast majority of vps4∆ mutants (>90% of cells, n = 121), the fluorescence of pHluorin-Atg8 was quenched in the vacuoles similar to WT cells, but occasionally few perivacuolar pHluorin-Atg8 positive structures were observed (<17% of cells, n = 121).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Autophagic bodies were efficiently lysed in acidified vacuoles of vps4∆ mutants.
source: Overall, it seemed that autophagic bodies were efficiently lysed in acidified vacuoles of vps4∆ mutants (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is inferred from the pHluorin-Atg8 quenching data.

claim: In yeast the autophagic machinery, the fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole per se and the lysis of autophagic bodies is not impaired in ESCRT mutants.
source: These findings emphasize that in yeast the autophagic machinery, the fusion of autophagosomes with the vacuole per se and the lysis of autophagic bodies is not impaired in ESCRT mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple autophagy assays in vps4∆ mutants.

claim: In total 2941 proteins were quantified (peptide count ≥ 2), comprising 58% of the characterized yeast ORFs.
source: In total 2941 proteins were quantified (peptide count ≥ 2), comprising 58% of the characterized yeast ORFs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, upper panel, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic analysis data.

claim: In the first 3 hr of starvation, the yeast proteome underwent extensive remodeling and 264 proteins significantly changed in abundance.
source: In this early phase of starvation, the yeast proteome already underwent extensive remodeling and 264 proteins significantly changed in abundance (MaxQuant significance B) (Cox and Mann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic analysis data.

claim: 101 proteins were significantly down- and 163 proteins significantly up-regulated during the first 3 hr of starvation.
source: 101 proteins were significantly down- and 163 proteins significantly up-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic analysis data.

claim: Amino acid- and carbohydrate-metabolic pathways were up-regulated to meet the demands of starving cells.
source: Amino acid- and carbohydrate-metabolic pathways were up-regulated to meet the demands of starving cells.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Most vacuolar hydrolases were up-regulated in response to nutrient limitation, indicating that starving cells enhanced the catabolic activity and thus the recycling capacity of their vacuoles.
source: Most vacuolar hydrolases were also up-regulated in response to nutrient limitation, indicating that starving cells enhanced the catabolic activity and thus the recycling capacity of their vacuoles.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data and inferred from the function of vacuolar hydrolases.

claim: Components of the autophagic machinery, including Atg1 and Atg8, were up-regulated during the first 3 hr of starvation.
source: Components of the autophagic machinery, including Atg1 and Atg8, were also up-regulated (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cell wall components, proteins required for ribosome biogenesis and cell cycle/division were down-regulated during the first 3 hr of starvation.
source: In contrast, cell wall components, proteins required for ribosome biogenesis and cell cycle/division were down-regulated (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Plasma membrane proteins were among the most frequently down-regulated cellular components during starvation.
source: Strikingly, the GO analysis also revealed that plasma membrane proteins were among the most frequently down-regulated cellular components during starvation.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Many plasma membrane proteins, including diverse high affinity nutrient permeases and the G-protein coupled receptor Ste2 were down-regulated during the first 3 hr of starvation.
source: Not only Mup1, but many other plasma membrane proteins, including diverse high affinity nutrient permeases required for the transport of sugars (Itr1, Hxt2, 3), nucleobases (Fur4), amino acids (Bap3, Gnp1, Tat1, Can1) and ammonium (Ato3) but also the G-protein coupled receptor Ste2 were down-regulated (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The starvation-induced remodeling of the plasma membrane was highly selective.
source: This comprehensive starvation-induced remodeling of the plasma membrane was highly selective.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential regulation of plasma membrane proteins.

claim: The protein levels of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase, Pma1, were not dramatically altered during starvation.
source: The protein levels of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase, Pma1, were not dramatically altered.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data and microscopy data.

claim: The general amino acid permease Gap1 and the ammonium permease Mep2 were strongly up-regulated during starvation.
source: Moreover, the general amino acid permease Gap1 and the ammonium permease Mep2 were strongly up-regulated and the majority of Gap1 was retained at the plasma membrane (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data and microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Correlation analysis (R = 0.82, p < 1e-16) revealed that WT cells and vps4∆ mutants up- or down-regulated similar proteins in response to starvation.
source: Correlation analysis (R = 0.82, p < 1e-16) revealed that WT cells and vps4∆ mutants up- or down-regulated similar proteins in response to starvation, suggesting that ESCRT mutants are not generally deficient in inducing a starvation response (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A majority of proteins in vps4∆ mutants showed less pronounced changes during starvation compared to WT cells.
source: However, data correlation analysis indicated that a majority of proteins in vps4∆ mutants showed less pronounced changes during starvation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The distribution of protein ratios was broader in WT cells than in the vps4∆ mutants (p < 6e-16).
source: This analysis showed that the distribution of protein ratios was broader in WT cells (blue curve) than in the vps4∆ mutants (green curve) (Figure 4C, p < 6e-16).
evidence: This is supported by density plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In WT cells more proteins were stronger up- or down-regulated under starvation compared to ESCRT mutants, where changes in protein levels were less pronounced.

source: It seems that the cellular defects of ESCRT mutants during starvation can be mostly attributed to their inability to degrade membrane proteins.

claim: A significant fraction of vacuolar hydrolases are sorted into the lumen of vacuoles in ESCRT mutants, where they mature and become active.
source: Furthermore, if the observed phenotypes in ESCRT mutants would be caused solely by mis-sorting of vacuolar hydrolases, this would lead to a delay in autophagy-mediated amino acid recycling. In this case their defects during starvation should be similar or even weaker when compared to autophagy mutants. The partial sorting defects for vacuolar hydrolases are thus not consistent with the stronger defects of ESCRT mutants in maintaining amino acid levels, protein synthesis and cell growth early during nutrient limitation. Moreover it was possible to restore the catabolic activity of vacuoles in ESCRT mutants under rich growth conditions, while this was no longer possible during starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes and the Vps10 overexpression experiments.

claim: Mainly the selective degradation of membrane proteins as a source for amino acids, rather than just the sorting of vacuolar hydrolases, contributes to the key role of the MVB pathway during starvation.
source: Hence it seems that mainly the selective degradation of membrane proteins as a source for amino acids, rather than just the sorting of vacuolar hydrolases, contributes to the key role of the MVB pathway during starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the Vps10 overexpression experiments and other data.

claim: Selective protein degradation may at least initially provide a bigger added value for the free intracellular amino acid pool as compared to the non-selective degradation of bulk cytoplasm by autophagy.
source: We speculate that membrane proteins that have been selected for degradation via the MVB are for the most part not re-synthesized, while non-selective autophagy will inevitably also capture and degrade proteins that are still needed and thus have to be replaced. Hence, selective protein degradation may at least initially provide a bigger added value for the free intracellular amino acid pool as compared to the non-selective degradation of bulk cytoplasm by autophagy.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why the MVB pathway is more critical early during starvation.

claim: The ESCRT machinery has been described to contribute to selective micro-autophagy on late endosomes in mammalian cells.
source: The ESCRT machinery has recently been described to contribute to selective micro-autophagy on late endosomes in mammalian cells (Sahu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Only the coordinated action of the MVB pathway and autophagy provides sufficient intracellular recycling capacity during starvation to allow efficient mitotic exit and entry into a stable G1/G0 quiescent state and thereby ensures cell survival.
source: Ultimately our results suggest that only the coordinated action of the MVB pathway and autophagy provides sufficient intracellular recycling capacity during starvation to allow efficient mitotic exit and entry into a stable G1/G0 quiescent state and thereby ensures cell survival (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle and survival data.

claim: The evolutionary conserved EGO/LAMTOR/Ragulator complex in conjugation with a lysosomal amino acid sensor could measure free amino acids in the lumen of lysosomes and transiently re-activate TORC1 to complete the final cell division cycle prior to entry into quiescence.
source: Alternatively, the evolutionary conserved EGO/LAMTOR/Ragulator complex in conjugation with a lysosomal amino acid sensor (Dubouloz et al., 2005; Sancak et al., 2010; Zoncu et al., 2011a; Rebsamen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015) could somehow measure free amino acids in the lumen of lysosomes and transiently re-activate TORC1 to complete the final cell division cycle prior to entry into quiescence (Matsui et al., 2013; An et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila and human cells, loss of the ESCRT machinery interferes with a late step in autophagy, namely the fusion of amphisomes with lysosomes.
source: In Drosophila and human cells, loss of the ESCRT machinery interferes with a late step in autophagy, namely the fusion of amphisomes with lysosomes (Nara et al., 2002; Filimonenko et al., 2007; Rusten et al., 2007; Lee and Gao, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Amphisomes are acidic pre-lysosomal hybrid organelles of MVBs/late endosomes and autophagosomes.
source: Amphisomes are acidic pre-lysosomal hybrid organelles of MVBs/late endosomes and autophagosomes (Stromhaug and Seglen, 1993)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A functional MVB pathway is key to boost the catabolic activity of MVB-derived amphisomes and thereby ensure the efficient degradation of autophagic cargo in higher eukaryotes.
source: Thus, our findings that a functional MVB pathway is key to boost the catabolic activity may not be restricted to lysosomes but may also include MVB-derived amphisomes and thereby ensure the efficient degradation of autophagic cargo in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning extending the findings to higher eukaryotes.

claim: In yeast autophagosomes appear to fuse directly with vacuoles and amphisomes have not been described.
source: In yeast autophagosomes appear to fuse directly with vacuoles and amphisomes have not been described.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast autophagy.

claim: Loss of ESCRT function does not significantly impair the autophagic machinery itself or the delivery of autophagic cargo into lysosomes in yeast or Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Consistently, we and others demonstrated that loss of ESCRT function does not significantly impair the autophagic machinery itself or the delivery of autophagic cargo into lysosomes in yeast or Caenorhabditis elegans (Reggiori et al., 2004; Djeddi et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by the data presented and citations to prior work.

claim: The MVB pathway takes a central role in cellular homeostasis to preserve and redistribute biomass that can be used to maintain cell growth under nutrient limitation.
source: Our results show that the MVB pathway takes a central role in cellular homeostasis to preserve and redistribute biomass that can be used to maintain cell growth under nutrient limitation.
evidence: This is inferred from all the data presented.

claim: During transient nutrient fluctuations or changes in metabolism a more stepwise activation of the catabolic cascade with initial selective protein degradation via UPS and the MVB pathway might help to delay massive non-selective breakdown of cytoplasm via autophagy.
source: It is tempting to speculate that during transient nutrient fluctuations or changes in metabolism a more stepwise activation of this catabolic cascade with initial selective protein degradation via UPS and the MVB pathway might help to delay massive non-selective breakdown of cytoplasm via autophagy, at least for some time.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: The stepwise activation of the catabolic cascade might provide a safety mechanism to protect cells from the immediate need for non-selective protein degradation.
source: This might provide a safety mechanism to protect cells from the immediate need for non-selective protein degradation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: The central role of the MVB pathway in the catabolic cascade of eukaryotic cells during starvation is evolutionary conserved.
source: While the ESCRT machinery has acquired additional roles in diverse biological processes in higher eukaryotes, we propose that the central role of the MVB pathway in the catabolic cascade of eukaryotic cells during starvation is evolutionary conserved.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings in yeast and knowledge of ESCRT functions.
